- Sparse FFN, Triton kernel I also work on optimising and speeding up model training with a sparse FFN, and for this I developed my own GPU kernel, written in Triton. In a model of 306 million parameters (FFN 4,096), the optimised kernel reached 36% higher throughput than its first version. Our early tests show that with a larger model and an FFN of 8,192, the sparse kernel from the EUGEN project can deliver a speed-up of more than 40% over a dense model. Whether a model trained sparse and densified at the end matches a dense model remains open, but the early results lead me to train the next, larger model this way. Kernel on Hugging Face Kernel code

- TetherGate: stabilising learned gates TetherGate is a mechanism that keeps learned gates from closing. A gate scaling a residual branch – an expert, an adapter or a newly added layer – tends to be pushed gradually to zero by the optimiser, after which the branch contributes nothing to the model. TetherGate combines a floor driven by the training step with a spring that pulls the gate's threshold towards a moving anchor computed from the current control signal. The signal can be any statistic. I have tested the mechanism experimentally in my own models. Download TetherGate (.zip) TetherGate on Hugging Face tethergate.py

- Independent research I keep doing my own research into artificial intelligence. I want to know whether we can find signals inside a model that will help us detect hallucinations or bad intentions. To that end, I study the activation signals of the model's internal layers, looking for indicators that would help predict and monitor such behaviour. - How I work with AI I don't write code by hand. I design the tasks and run teams of AI agents, and I check every result. A team works in three stages: research, execution and verification. Execution is overseen by two independent controllers: one keeps to the scope of the task, the other to its technical quality. I run two or three such teams in parallel, so when one task needs my attention, the others keep going. I delegate large chunks of work, but only up to the point where I can still check them properly. Whether something is done is decided by tests or measurements, not by the model's claim. team.txt

…I have no formal education in programming or in training LLMs.

I got into building apps and training AI through a thoroughly strange chain of coincidences which, looking back, seems to make quite a lot of sense. And I think it says something important about our times. I hadn’t planned it; I never imagined I’d have more to do with technology than the average iPhone user. For years my only window onto the world of Big Tech was the Hard Fork podcast. Shout-out to Casey and Kevin :)

It all started with vibe coding and the OrsonAI app. Playing around with AI, I began building tools that could help me in my day-to-day work as a journalist. Transcribing interviews while they were being recorded and importing them into an editor, or an editing mode that let me consult a chatbot about selected passages without switching windows and pasting in the whole context — at the time these were genuinely neat tools, and they sped my work up considerably.

Over time I began to think of it as a project, something that could serve other people too. The idea was simple: take the features that save me time and build a product for people facing the same problems. I spent a lot of time building an interface and mechanisms that could deliver safe AI for newsrooms — AI that helps the journalist but doesn’t do the job for them. I even designed a system that issues certificates of human authorship for a text, published on the Hedera Hashgraph public ledger. An immutable record with evidentiary value in court, showing how the text came into being and what part a human played in writing it.

But I was in for a big disappointment. The reception from the industry people I showed the app to was frosty, to say the least. The question that came up at the end of every presentation made me painfully aware of how wrong I’d been: “Why would anyone pay for your app when we’ve got ChatGPT for free?” Things like a certificate of human authorship, data protection or even a substantial improvement in workflow over what an ordinary chatbot offered didn’t matter. I heard this from people who, day in, day out, stress the importance of reliable journalism.

Still, working on the app, and on an agentic AI system reliable enough to be used in newsrooms, pushed me in a completely new direction. Trying to understand better where language-model hallucinations come from, I started reading research papers on arXiv, and eventually designed and ran a series of studies on SwiGLU gate activations in several open language models. I wrote up the findings in a few papers that I posted on ResearchGate.
